Augustine on Time
Peter Grant
CH 501
April 28, 2026
Augustine's meditation on time in Book XI of the Confessions begins with a confession of
ignorance. "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know."1 The sentence is famous because
it is honest; it names a problem that philosophers still argue about.
For Augustine, the past no longer exists and the future does not yet exist; only the present
is real, and even the present has no extension.2 Time, he concludes, must be a distension of
the mind itself.
1. Augustine, Confessions, trans. Henry Chadwick (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991), 230.
2. Ibid., 232.
Grant 2
This conclusion is often read as a precursor to Kant. That reading may be anachronistic, but
it is not entirely wrong; both thinkers locate time in the knowing subject.3
3. Paul Ricoeur, Time and Narrative, vol. 1 (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984), 7-12.
Bibliography
Augustine. Confessions. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991.
Ricoeur, Paul. Time and Narrative. Vol. 1. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984.
